one_liner: Capture and qualify the trigger — is this worth a look?
description: Something surfaced — a support theme, a lost deal, a telemetry anomaly, an exec hunch, a regulatory change — and someone has to log it, deduplicate it against what's already known, and decide it deserves attention at all. Agents increasingly do the sweeping and clustering across tickets, calls and analytics; a human still judges which clusters are real.

one_liner: Set the question, timebox and riskiest assumptions to test
description: Write down what you're trying to learn, what you'd have to believe for this to be worth doing, and how long you're prepared to spend finding out. This is where assumption mapping happens, so research targets the risky unknowns instead of confirming the comfortable ones. Humans set the question and timebox; agents draft the assumption list and propose cheap tests.

one_liner: Who cares, who decides, who can kill it — and the sponsor
description: Identify the people whose problem this is, whose budget it touches, whose systems it crosses, and who holds the veto — then secure a named sponsor willing to own the decision at the end. Discovery that skips this produces well-evidenced work nobody has standing to act on. Almost entirely human relationship work.

one_liner: Size the segments, the money and the regulatory ground
description: Establish who has this problem beyond your own walls, how many of them there are, what they spend today, and what rules govern the space. It stops a real-but-tiny problem being mistaken for a market. This is the job agents have taken over most completely — desk research, sizing arithmetic and source collation are agent-drafted, human-audited.

one_liner: What people hire today — rivals, spreadsheets, doing nothing
description: Catalogue every current answer to the job: competing products, the incumbent SaaS, the export-to-Excel workaround, and plain living with it. The bar to clear is the best existing alternative plus switching cost, not zero. Agents crawl competitor material at scale; humans observe the workarounds nobody documents.

one_liner: First-hand evidence of the struggle, in their words
description: Talk to the people who live the problem and the people who'd pay to fix it — what they're trying to get done, what they've tried and abandoned, what triggered the search. This is the evidence that separates a real opportunity from a plausible one. Humans run the conversations; agents handle recruiting, transcription and cross-interview pattern extraction.

one_liner: Telemetry, tickets and CRM — how common is the struggle?
description: Interrogate the evidence you already own — product analytics, support tickets, sales-loss reasons, ops logs — to quantify how widespread and expensive the problem actually is. It's the counterweight to interviews: frequency and cost where interviews give why. Largely agent-executed, with humans deciding which cohorts and time windows are honest.

one_liner: Data, integration, compliance and cost reality checks
description: Run cheap probes on the hard constraints before framing an opportunity around them: does the data exist, does that system have an API, what does privacy or accreditation demand, is the unit cost plausible. Agents can build a throwaway spike in hours, which has pulled feasibility evidence forward from planning into discovery.

one_liner: Fake doors, pre-sales, pilots — will anyone actually move?
description: Put something in front of real people that costs them something to respond to — a landing page, a concierge run, a priced pre-sale — and measure behaviour rather than opinion. This catches the enthusiastic interview that would never convert. Humans own the offer and the ask; agents stand up the test assets and instrument results in days, not a quarter.

one_liner: Turn raw research into patterns, themes and confidence
description: Pull every strand — interviews, data, market, alternatives, probes — into a single view: what the evidence supports, what it contradicts, what's still unknown, and how confident you are in each. Agents do the heavy clustering and contradiction-spotting; humans own the judgement about what the pattern means and where the evidence is thin.
depends_on: market-scan alternatives-map user-research data-mining feasibility-probe demand-test

one_liner: One statement: who, what struggle, why now, what success is
description: Write the crisp statement of the problem: whose it is, what the struggle costs them, why now, what the current alternative is, and what observable change would mean you'd solved it. This framing is the anchor every downstream job traces back to. Human-authored, with agents stress-testing the wording against the evidence base.

one_liner: Go / no-go: worth defining, park it, or kill it
description: The sponsor and stakeholders look at the framed opportunity and the evidence behind it and decide: take it into definition, park it with a trigger to revisit, or kill it out loud. It's the cheapest place to stop, and actually killing things here keeps the rest of the pipeline honest. Irreducibly human — accountability for a bet can't be delegated.

one_liner: Turn intent into a testable, delegable specification
description: Convert the framed opportunity into requirements precise enough to hand to an agent and testable enough to verify later — stories, rules, acceptance criteria, edge cases, out-of-scope. This is the delegable artifact of the agentic SDLC: you cannot delegate what you cannot define. Agent-drafted from research, then interrogated by a human who owns the ambiguity.

one_liner: Performance, security, accessibility and compliance bars
description: Name the non-functional bars the solution must clear — latency, privacy and security posture, accessibility level, regulatory obligations — as measurable targets rather than aspirations. Left implicit, these surface as expensive rework after the build. A human call by leads and compliance stakeholders, with agents drafting the checklist from applicable standards.

one_liner: Decide what it looks like and how it behaves end to end
description: Turn the requirements into an experience: the flows, screens, states, error and empty cases, and how it fits the existing product. Decisions made here are cheap; the same decisions discovered mid-build by an agent guessing are not. Human-led for the hard judgement calls, with agents generating variants and pattern-consistent screens at speed.

one_liner: Copy, taxonomy, data model and what must be migrated
description: Specify the substance the software moves around: the domain model and key entities, data contracts, migration and seeding needs, plus UI copy and terminology. Vague data definitions are the most common cause of agents building something plausible but wrong. Shared between content designers, domain SMEs and agents.

one_liner: Put a clickable draft in front of real users before build
description: Test the proposed solution — not the problem — with a prototype or walkthrough, and fold what breaks back into the spec and design. When agents can produce a working prototype in hours, validating the definition before committing is close to free and stops teams building the wrong right thing. Agents build it; humans run the sessions and read the reactions.

one_liner: Name the numbers that will say whether this worked
description: Agree the outcome measures, baselines, targets and time horizon before anything is built, plus the counter-metrics that would say it went wrong. Without this the release can never be judged and the business case is unfalsifiable. Human-owned; agents propose candidate metrics and check the instrumentation exists to collect them.

one_liner: Cost, benefit and payback period for doing it at all
description: Attach numbers to the definition: build and run cost — now including agent inference spend and review effort — expected benefit, payback period and the risk of doing nothing. This is the artifact the funder judges, and what kills zombie projects before they consume a quarter. Agents assemble the model and sensitivity ranges from delivery telemetry.

one_liner: Choose the first slice and sequence what waits
description: Cut the definition into the smallest release that tests the case, and sequence the rest — what ships now, what is deferred, what is explicitly never. This scope is what the plan gate approves and what verification later holds the build to. A human trade-off call; agents size the options and expose dependencies between slices.

one_liner: Walk owners through scope and settle trade-offs early
description: Take the spec, design and scope to the people who will be affected — support, sales, ops, legal, dependent teams — and resolve objections while they are cheap to absorb. Misalignment discovered after the build is the most common cause of a finished release that cannot ship. Almost entirely human; agents tailor the walkthrough material and track open issues.

one_liner: Human sign-off on scope and case before planning starts
description: A decision gate: an accountable human approves the spec, scope, success metrics and business case as the baseline the team will plan and build against. Saying no or descoping here costs a conversation; saying it after agents have built costs the release. Strictly human — the gate exists precisely because the work either side of it is increasingly delegated.

one_liner: Architecture and approach for how it gets built
description: Translate the agreed scope and design into a technical approach: system and data architecture, key interfaces, reuse vs build, and the significant trade-offs with their rationale. These choices are cheap to change now and expensive once agents are building against them. Agent-drafted from the spec and codebase, then argued over and shaped by a tech lead.

one_liner: Find the unknowns that could break the plan
description: Name the things that could sink the delivery — unproven integrations, performance unknowns, security exposure, legacy landmines, agent capability limits — and decide which need a timeboxed spike before commitment. Unexamined risk is what turns an approved plan into a mid-build rewrite. Agents surface candidate risks; humans judge severity and appetite.

one_liner: Encode conventions, compliance and definition of done
description: Write the engineering constitution the build must obey: context files (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md), coding and architectural conventions, security and regulatory constraints, and an explicit definition of done. This is what lets delegated build run fast without drifting — the rules are machine-readable rather than tribal. Agent-drafted from repo patterns, hardened by a senior engineer.

one_liner: Agent-drafted, human-shaped delegable units of work
description: Decompose the approach into task-level work packets sized and bounded for delegation — each with its slice of the spec, its acceptance criteria, its blast radius and its dependencies. This is the artefact agents actually build against, so vague packets produce vague code. Agents draft; a tech lead reshapes boundaries and decides what runs in parallel.

one_liner: Decide how each task will be proven done
description: Decide up front how the build will be proven correct: which layers get automated tests, what needs evals or golden datasets, what needs manual checking, and what evidence a reviewer will see at the diff boundary. Verification is where most human effort now lands — designing it after the build starts is how teams end up trusting output they cannot check.

one_liner: Third-party access, data, licences and approvals
description: Secure everything the build needs from outside the team: vendor and API accounts, credentials and sandbox access, test data and its privacy clearance, licences, and any approvals with lead times. These are the classic silent blockers — a fleet of agents can be idled for a week by one unissued API key. Almost entirely human chasing.

one_liner: Size the work and order it into a delivery sequence
description: Put shape and order on the breakdown: rough sizing (including agent-run and review time, not just build time), the critical path, what runs in parallel, and the milestones the release will be tracked against. The plan gate is where commitments get made, and an unsequenced backlog is not a commitment. Agents produce the first pass; a delivery lead applies judgement.

one_liner: Repos, CI, sandboxes and test data ready to run
description: Stand up the machinery the build runs inside: repositories and branching model, CI pipelines with checks already wired, isolated sandboxes, seeded test data, and observability from day one. Preparation here is what makes unattended, parallel, overnight agent work possible instead of a stream of broken runs.

one_liner: Permissions, spend caps and agent context wired up
description: Configure how agents will actually work: which tools, MCP servers and repos they can touch, what they may do unattended versus with approval, secrets handling, and spend limits per workstream. It matters twice over — it is the security boundary for autonomous code execution, and token burn is real delivery cost that goes unnoticed until the margin is gone.

one_liner: Who builds, who reviews, and how much review capacity
description: Assign ownership across the plan — who orchestrates which workstream, who holds the reviewer seat for each area, who is accountable at each gate — and sanity-check that review bandwidth can absorb the volume the agents will produce. Reviewer capacity, not build capacity, is the binding constraint in an agentic pipeline.

one_liner: Human sign-off before the build is delegated
description: The hard gate before delegation: accountable humans review the approach, breakdown, sequence, risks, guardrails and cost, and explicitly approve, redirect or descope before implementation is delegated. It is the cheapest point to say no, and the last one before agents start producing code at volume. Agents prepare the pack and flag gaps in it.
depends_on: tech-approach task-breakdown estimate-sequence tech-risk verify-strategy capacity-plan

one_liner: Turn plan tasks into agent-ready work orders and assign
description: Convert each task into a self-contained work order: scope boundaries, context pointers, acceptance criteria, allowed tools and the definition of done — then decide what goes to an agent, what stays human, and what runs in parallel. Bad briefs are the single largest cause of wasted agent runs, so this is where most of the leverage sits.

one_liner: Write tests, evals and acceptance checks agents run against
description: Translate the spec's intent into machine-checkable form — unit, integration and contract tests, evals for non-deterministic behaviour, and assertions that encode the acceptance criteria. This is what lets agents iterate unsupervised, so it goes first or alongside implementation. Agents draft the bulk; a senior engineer confirms the checks test intent, not implementation.

one_liner: Seeds, golden files and stubs for third-party dependencies
description: Produce the data and doubles the checks need: synthetic seed datasets, golden files, recorded fixtures, and stubs for external services. Without realistic fixtures the feedback loop is either too weak to catch defects or too flaky to steer agents. Agents generate most of it; humans rule on realism and privacy.

one_liner: Agents write the code, iterating until checks go green
description: The actual construction: agents in isolated environments write and refactor code against the executable spec, looping on compiler, lint, test and eval feedback until checks pass. Volume here is now mostly agent output; humans hand-write the small, high-risk or high-ambiguity slices and set the taste agents copy. The output is many candidate branches, not one.

one_liner: Schema changes, backfills and reversible migration scripts
description: Change the data model and write the migration path: forward and rollback scripts, expand/contract sequencing, backfills, and compatibility windows so old and new code can run side by side. Separated from ordinary implementation because it is the least reversible thing in the change-set — and where agents most often produce something that works in test and destroys data in production.

one_liner: Settle interfaces, upstream blockers and package upgrades
description: Chase down everything the build needs from outside its own boundary: interface contracts with adjacent teams, API stubs so work can proceed, library upgrades, and escalating third-party blockers. Parallel agent work multiplies interface friction, so unresolved contracts stall whole fleets. Mostly human coordination, with agents drafting contract specs and mocks.

one_liner: Watch runs, kill bad branches, retry, hold cost in budget
description: Operate the fleet while it runs: monitor progress and token spend per task, spot agents thrashing or drifting off-scope, kill dead-end branches early, re-brief and retry, and pick winners when several agents attempt the same task. Inference spend is now delivery cost — unmanaged fleets quietly burn margin and produce plausible-looking rubbish.

one_liner: Merge parallel branches, fix conflicts, keep trunk green
description: Bring the parallel branches together into one coherent change-set: rebase and merge in a sane order, resolve textual and semantic conflicts, reconcile duplicated abstractions that separate agents invented, and keep the integration branch green. This is the classic bottleneck of parallel agentic build, where volume converts into merge pain.

one_liner: Update CLAUDE.md, ADRs, API docs and runbooks as you build
description: Keep the artefacts that steer future agents and humans in step with the code: agent context files, architecture decision records, API and schema docs, runbook edits. Stale context files degrade every subsequent agent run, so this is maintenance of the production system rather than paperwork. Agents draft the diffs; a human approves guardrail changes.

one_liner: Burn-up against plan, surface blockers, report status
description: Maintain a truthful picture of where the build actually is: what has landed, what is in flight, what is blocked, spend to date, and confidence against the agreed dates. With agents running overnight and in parallel, task boards go stale fast — status has to be derived from the repo and run telemetry. Delivery leads own the narrative; agents assemble the roll-up.

one_liner: Decide when a build discovery changes scope or approach
description: When the build uncovers something the plan didn't anticipate — a wrong assumption, a hidden dependency, a spec ambiguity only visible in code — a human decides whether to absorb it, change approach, cut scope, or stop and re-plan. The one real decision gate inside the build, and the moment agents cannot self-authorise. Agents surface the discovery with options and impact.

one_liner: Assemble the reviewable diff and its story for Verify
description: Turn the integrated branch into something a reviewer and the verification gates can consume: coherent commits, a change description explaining intent and trade-offs, links to spec and plan, migration notes, and a self-review pass that strips debug scaffolding and dead agent artefacts. Review bandwidth is the scarce resource downstream — a well-packaged diff is what makes verification affordable.

one_liner: CI, test suites and evals turn the change-set into evidence
description: Execute the full verification harness against the integrated change-set: unit, integration and contract tests, static analysis, and eval suites for any model-driven behaviour. This is the bulk of verification effort and the point where 'it works' stops being an opinion and becomes an artifact. Almost fully automated; humans own the harness thresholds.

one_liner: Agent refutes the change against the spec before a human looks
description: A fresh-context reviewer agent reads the diff and tries to break it: unrequested scope, silent behaviour changes, drift from the spec, dead or duplicated code, missing coverage on the changed paths. It exists to protect the scarcest resource in the loop — senior review attention — by filtering the obvious before the human gate.

one_liner: Dependency, secret and SAST scans plus data-handling review
description: Clear the change for security risk: dependency and CVE scanning, hallucinated-package checks, secret detection, SAST/DAST, and a judgement pass on authn/authz in the changed paths. Agent-generated code raises the base rate of plausible-but-wrong security decisions, so this stops being an occasional audit and becomes a per-change gate.

one_liner: Prove it holds under expected and peak load, including data
description: Run load, stress, soak and query-plan tests against a production-like environment, including rehearsing migrations at realistic data volumes. Performance regressions are the classic thing a green test suite hides, and agent-authored code is prone to N+1s and quietly expensive calls. Rig execution is automated; reading the results against budgets stays human.

one_liner: Automated WCAG checks plus real assistive-tech walkthroughs
description: Verify the change against accessibility standards: automated axe/WCAG scans in CI, then manual keyboard, screen-reader and contrast walkthroughs of the changed flows. Automated tooling catches perhaps half the real defects, so the manual pass is not optional where the change touches UI.

one_liner: Show the change meets regulatory and contractual obligations
description: Confirm the change satisfies whatever regime applies — privacy and data residency, PCI, APRA CPS 234, SOC 2 change-control, licence obligations on new dependencies — and capture the artefacts an auditor will later ask for. Agents assemble the control evidence and flag likely issues; a compliance owner signs the interpretation.

one_liner: Collate results into proof a reviewer can act on quickly
description: Pull the scattered outputs — test and eval results, coverage deltas, scan reports, performance numbers, spec-conformance notes — into one readable summary of what was checked, what passed, and what is still open. Without it the human gate degrades into rubber-stamping, because nobody can hold twenty tool outputs in their head.

one_liner: Experienced engineer judges the change at the PR boundary
description: An experienced engineer reads the change-set alongside the evidence pack and decides whether it is fit to proceed — checking intent, design fit, maintainability and the things no test encodes. As of 2026 this is the universal hard gate: everything upstream can be delegated, this cannot. Agents supply summaries and context to make the judgement cheaper.

one_liner: Confirm it does the job the spec and metrics described
description: Exercise the change against the acceptance criteria and the success metrics defined upstream — functional end-to-end flows, business rules, and the measurable outcome the work was justified by. This is where you catch software that passes every unit test and still does the wrong job.

one_liner: Hunt the failures nobody thought to write a test for
description: Unscripted, curiosity-led testing in a realistic environment: odd inputs, interrupted flows, stale sessions, permission edges, the seams between this change and everything around it. Scripted verification only finds what someone anticipated, and agent-written tests inherit the same blind spots as agent-written code. Still predominantly human.

one_liner: Business owners and real users try it and sign off
description: Put the change in front of the people who will live with it — business owners, support, a slice of real users — with realistic data, and get an explicit accept-or-reject. The last chance to discover the requirement was right and the interpretation was wrong; in client work it is usually the contractual sign-off. Irreducibly human.

one_liner: Judge severity, decide ship-blockers, send fixes to build
description: Take everything verification surfaced — failed checks, review comments, scan findings, UAT defects — deduplicate, judge severity and decide what blocks the release versus what is logged and lived with. This is the control loop back into build, where verification volume either gets managed or drowns the team. Agents cluster, reproduce and draft fixes; the ship-blocker call stays human.

one_liner: Build artifacts, version, tag and sign the change-set
description: Assemble the verified change-set into one immutable shippable unit: build the artifacts, apply version and tags, generate the SBOM and provenance, sign and publish. Everything downstream — rollback, audit, incident forensics — depends on there being exactly one identifiable thing that shipped. Almost entirely automated; humans own the versioning policy.

one_liner: Rehearse and sequence schema and data changes for cutover
description: Prepare the state change that ships alongside the code: rehearse the migration against a production-shaped dataset, confirm expand/contract sequencing so versions can coexist, and estimate the cutover window. The single most common source of un-rollbackable releases. Agents dry-run competently; a senior engineer owns the sequencing decision and watches the run.

one_liner: Decide how to undo this before you need to
description: Write down how this specific release gets undone: revert path, flag kill-switch, data repair steps for anything irreversible, the trigger conditions that mean 'pull it', and who is allowed to call it. Without this the go/no-go is a guess and the first bad signal becomes an improvised incident. Agents draft; a human owns the irreversibility judgement.

one_liner: Flags, cohorts and canary steps for a controlled ramp
description: Set up how the change reaches users rather than whether it exists: feature flag states, canary and cohort definitions, ramp percentages and dwell times, and success/abort thresholds at each step. Decoupling deploy from release turns a risky big-bang into a reversible experiment. Choosing who sees it first is a human product-and-risk decision.

one_liner: Agree timing, freeze windows and who is on deck
description: Coordinate when this actually goes: a slot that respects change freezes, peak trading, dependent teams' releases and regional hours — and confirm who is rostered for the deploy and the hours after. Timing is where most release pain is avoided or created, and the job most often skipped by fast-moving teams.

one_liner: Turn the changelog into what changed and why it matters
description: Produce the human-readable record: a generated changelog reconciled against the actual change-set, rewritten as what users, support and auditors need to know — new behaviour, fixes, breaking changes, required actions. Agents draft this well from commits and the diff; a human edits for accuracy on breaking changes and for tone.

one_liner: Refresh help, API and in-product content to match
description: Bring every user-facing surface into line with the new behaviour: help articles, API reference, in-product tooltips, screenshots, admin runbooks. Documentation that lags the release generates support load and quietly erodes trust. Docs agents diff the API surface and propose edits; a writer reviews anything customer-visible.

one_liner: Arm support, sales and ops before users arrive
description: Give the people who face users what they need before the release lands: what changed, expected questions, known issues and workarounds, escalation path, who to page during the window. A release that surprises your own support desk becomes a customer-visible failure regardless of code quality.

one_liner: Draft external comms, staged for the go decision
description: Get the outward-facing communication ready but not sent: customer email or in-app notice, status-page entries, marketing copy, advance warning for breaking changes. Preparing before the gate means the announcement ships with the release — and can be held instantly if the gate says no. Approval to send is human and withheld until deploy succeeds.

one_liner: Go / no-go with evidence, risk and rollback on the table
description: The hard human gate: someone accountable reviews the verification evidence, residual risk, rollback plan and timing, then says ship or hold. Exposing real users to a change is an accountability act, not a computation — often the only remaining point where a human takes ownership of what goes live. Agents assemble the evidence; the signature is human.

one_liner: Execute the cutover and ramp the rollout as planned
description: Execute the plan: promote the artifact, run the migrations at the agreed point, advance the rollout through its canary and cohort steps, and abort to the rollback path if thresholds are breached. Mechanically automated — pipelines and deployment agents drive it — with a named human watching and holding the abort call.

one_liner: Smoke-test the live system before declaring it done
description: Confirm the deployed system actually works in production: critical-path smoke tests, synthetic transactions, migration integrity spot-checks, and comparison of key signals against the pre-deploy baseline. The difference between 'the deploy succeeded' and 'the release works' — and what decides whether the rollout ramps, holds or reverts.

one_liner: Comms, onboarding and training so the release lands
description: Make the release actually land with the people it was built for: send the announcement, run onboarding and training, update in-product guidance, make sure frontline support can answer questions on day one. Software nobody adopts did not really ship, and adoption is what every downstream measurement depends on.

one_liner: Watch production signals against agreed thresholds
description: Watch the release in production against its SLOs — errors, latency, saturation, business-critical funnels — and alert when reality diverges from expectation. The first honest feedback the release gets; in a loop that turns in hours it is the only safety net fast enough to matter. Agents watch and correlate; humans set thresholds and decide what's worth waking up for.

one_liner: Decide if the release stays in or gets pulled
description: After the soak period, someone accountable looks at the health signals and early usage and decides: promote to full rollout, hold at the current ramp, or execute the rollback plan. The last cheap moment to undo a bad release before it becomes load-bearing. Agents assemble the evidence and can auto-revert on hard breaches; the ambiguous call stays human.

one_liner: Detect, mitigate and communicate when it breaks
description: When production breaks, restore service: triage severity, mitigate, keep stakeholders and affected users informed, hand over cleanly across time zones. Speed of mitigation, not elegance of fix, is the job. Agents do much of first response — log correlation, hypothesis generation, drafting patches — while incident command stays with a named human.

one_liner: Turn each incident into a durable fix, not a war story
description: Reconstruct what happened and why, blamelessly, and convert it into concrete changes: missing tests, missing alerts, missing guardrails, missing context in the spec. Without this the same incident recurs at agent speed and volume. Agents draft the timeline from telemetry; humans own the causal reasoning and which actions are worth doing.

one_liner: Sort inbound noise into fixes, specs and known issues
description: Work the inbound queue: reproduce reported bugs, separate defects from misunderstandings from genuine feature requests, set severity, and route each item into a fix, a next-cycle spec or a documented known issue. This is where users tell you what the release actually got wrong. Agents handle first-pass classification and reproduction; humans arbitrate severity.

one_liner: Dependencies, CVEs, cost and drift kept under control
description: Keep the running system healthy between releases: security patches, dependency and platform upgrades, certificate rotation, data hygiene, cloud cost and performance drift. Unglamorous, continuous, and the thing that quietly decides whether the codebase stays delegable to agents. Agents open and verify routine upgrade PRs; humans approve anything risky.

one_liner: See what users actually do, not what you hoped
description: Instrument and read the behavioural evidence: adoption and activation, funnel drop-off, feature usage, NPS and direct qualitative feedback, plus themes from support. The difference between shipping a feature and knowing whether it worked. Agents aggregate continuously; humans pick the questions worth answering and interrogate the surprises.

one_liner: Judge the business case on real numbers: keep, pivot, kill
description: Hold the release against the success metrics and business case it was funded on, and make the call: double down, adjust, or stop. This is the gate that stops a team cheerfully iterating on something that never moved a number. Agents produce the measurement; the keep-pivot-kill decision is an accountable human one — it reallocates money and people.

one_liner: Inspect how the loop itself ran, not just what shipped
description: Retro the delivery process rather than the product: where the spec was ambiguous, where agents went off-track, where review became the bottleneck, how long the loop actually took, what the rework rate was. In an agentic SDLC the process is a product you are also iterating on. Agents supply cycle-time and rework data; the honest conversation is human.

one_liner: Diff lessons back into context files, skills and evals
description: Turn the cycle's lessons into durable changes to the machinery: update context and steering files, tighten or add evals, adjust verification harnesses and autonomy policy, retire skills that misfired. Without it every cycle starts from the same place and the agents never get better at this codebase. A human approves the diff, exactly like a code change.

one_liner: Validated learning becomes the next cycle's intent
description: Convert everything production taught you — outcome data, usage patterns, support themes, unmet needs, deferred bugs — into framed opportunities and candidate requirements for the next loop, with the evidence attached. This is the join that makes the SDLC a loop rather than a line; in 2026 it closes in days rather than quarters. Humans decide what earns a place in the next cycle.
